utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The screens. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am trying to take advantage of this break as we are waiting for the witness, to raise an issue on behalf of the Defence team he is. This is that we discussed yesterday, and it is not entirely clear to us. I will put to you now the position of the Defence in view of Rule 90(H) and I would like for us to receive instructions from you, from the Trial Chamber, as to whether our position is correct or not. Yesterday we discussed, based on the objection raised by my learned friend in relation to the cross-examination of Mr. Borovic and also in relation to Rule 90(H), item (ii), and the obligation of the Defence to put to the witness the nature of their defence in relation to questions put to the witness in cross-examination. The Defence believes that Rule 90(H) which regulates the manner and scope of cross-examination is designed in such a way that the obligation mentioned under item (ii) only pertains to a case when cross-examination is outside of the topics covered in examination-in-chief, and is about the facts concerning which a witness can give a relevant statement in relation to the position of the examining party. It is opinion of the Defence that, based on this, it means that if Defence is cross-examining a witness about issues raised within examination-in-chief, or if they're examining a witness in relation to his or her credibility, then the Defence is not duty-bound to put its position to the witness. As for 90(H)(ii) which, in view of the Defence pertains to this special case of cross-examination which covers topics outside of examination-in-chief, we believe that it was included within the rule in order to regulate in these special circumstances of cross-examination any situations in which a witness could be tricked whereby he would not be informed of the position of the Defence and that this creates a fair environment between the witness and the examining counsel. This is not a matter that concerns Prosecution in any way. Our position is that these provisions do not pertain to those parts of cross-examination which are covered by examination-in-chief or verifying the credibility of the witness. Your Honours, I would like to know whether we are correct or not in interpreting it in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The position, Mr. Vasic, is different from your understanding. The two provisions of the Rule, subparagraphs (i) and (ii) stand separately. (i) is talking about the normal case, and it is, in fact, limiting the range of cross-examination that can be made by a witness, limiting, say, Defence to what is dealt with in evidence in chief and the matter of credibility. Subsection (ii) or subparagraph (ii) of (H) is dealing with a separate and distinct and additional subject. And what it is saying is that you not only may, but you shall, it is an obligation, put to a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to your case, the parts of your case that appear to be different from, that appear to contradict the evidence of that witness. So if you've got a witness who's talking about something that's relevant to your case and the evidence of that witness appears to be in some way different from your case, in short your obligation is to put to that witness the essence of your case so that the witness has an opportunity to comment on the difference between the case as you see it and the case as the witness -- or it's not the case, but that the evidence of the witness about those circumstances. So this isn't in any way limited by subsection -- by subparagraph (i) of paragraph (H). It's additional and separate, and the object is to ensure that the witness is in a position and is given the opportunity to comment on what will be your evidence and your different case when you come to call it. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. It is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very brief. Perhaps it is clear to my friend Vasic, but it is not clear to me and I will explain briefly why not. I understand this when it comes to the issues raised in examination-in-chief. Yesterday we had a very specific case. The Prosecutor reacted claiming that I have to put to the witness something in relation to the information conveyed about Zoran from Karaburma. If we discuss this in examination-in-chief and in cross, I do not think that I still need to put the position of the Defence to this witness. Notwithstanding your explanation, perhaps we're speaking of two different things and perhaps yesterday the Prosecutor made a mistake when it comes to that specific example. Therefore, if the matter does not involve a new issue, but rather an issue raised in examination-in-chief and in cross, do we still have to, in accordance with Rule 90 (H) (ii), to put our case to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, is the short answer, Mr. Borovic. If you, in your cross-examination, don't get to put your case, the fact that you have asked some questions about it isn't good enough. You've got to go there step further and make clear where your case is materially different from his evidence. And that way there is an opportunity then for the witness to comment on the different case that you have. Now, yesterday I think it's probably fair to say that Mr. Smith didn't give your cross-examination full measure. You probably had gone far enough. But we cleared that up, so don't use yesterday as a complete example of what this is about. But you've got to put your case. Can I try and think of a quick example? A witness is called who says, "yes, I saw accused X here and there, two places." And you might cross-examine his evidence about when he says he saw the accused X in those two places. If it is part of your case that actually he saw accused X on a third occasion, which he hasn't spoken about, you've got to put to him that there was also a third occasion which he hasn't mentioned in his examination-in-chief. Understand that? Yeah. Okay. Now, Mr. Moore, you've been left out of this, not by design, but is there anything that I have left unsaid that ought to be said that you would submit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, thank you. That is our understanding of the articles. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, thank you then. I understand, Mr. Berghofer has been here and has been waiting patiently. Could you please stand, sir? If you would take the card and read aloud the affirmation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Dragutin Berghofer, nicknamed Beli.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would you be kind enough, please, to tell us your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: 29th of October 1940.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how would you describe your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, I was always recorded as a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To assist the Court, this witness, I hope, will be giving evidence in relation to the hospital, the JNA barracks, Ovcara and Velepromet. I want to deal, if I may, please, in very general terms. What was your involvement in Vukovar in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: In November 1991 I worked in the logistics. Do you need the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if you can tell us how long you were involved in logistics, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to start from the 24th of August. It was then that I left my house because the JNA had destroyed, had razed to the ground 120 metres of residential premises for which I had a 20-year mortgage. So the last day I was in my house was the 24th of August. It was right next to the barracks. And then I went down to another house I had, where I had a commercial premises. This was in an area called Slavija, 400 metres from the barracks. This is where I spent the rest of my time in Vukovar, until the 17th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I may come back to deal with that period subsequently, but let us move on in time to the 17th of November. On the 17th of November, did you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: On the 17th of November we went into what we called a break-through. We wanted to leave Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you succeed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, we did not. Because up there -- how should I describe it, they started killing us. I was all scared and there were another five people with me, so we returned to the hospital. 30 minutes before the midnight ushering in the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How many of you had been involved in the attempted break-out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Since I grew up in that area near the hospital, I led the column. There were almost 350 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many people went back to the hospital? Can you give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Marko Mandic, his wife, Dr. Aleksijevic, his wife, Jofra [phoen] Jankovic, and myself, as far as I can remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just then deal -- again, I'm trying to move on in time, but when you were at the hospital do you remember the JNA and other military forces arriving at the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: The first I saw him -- saw them was on the 19th of November at around 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people who came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Since I was in a room together with Dr. Ivankovic and a couple of other doctors, I peeked out and I noticed Bogdan Kuzmic with young soldiers. They were questioning Stanko Duvnjak who had been wounded, and I remember well that Stanko said, "What could I do?" And obviously I retreated straight away back into the room, and I didn't come out again until the next day, the 20th, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal with the form of the questioning of Stanko? Can you give the court a picture of what was happening at that time and the general atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He was sitting, because he had been wounded, and so he was wearing his pyjamas, and Kuzmic, surrounded by two young soldiers, was there, and the only thing I heard was the words, "And what could I do?" That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on then in time, if we may. You said you didn't come out again until the next day, the 20th, so let us move on to the 20th of November, please. When was it that you came out on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: On the 20th in the morning at around 7.00 a.m. I was saying hello to Dr. Ivankovic and a tall officer came along, he had a booming voice, and he was a tall man, and he said, "Doctor, what are we waiting for? It's -- we're at war. The wounded as well as civilians should go to the left and the hospital staff to the right." So basically it meant that the hospital staff had to go through the main gates of the hospital as you come from the Lola Ribar street and the rest of us, we had to go to the left, which was called Sapudl, but I think it's a different name, Abozida [phoen] or something. At any rate, the lightly wounded and the civilians were supposed to go out through the side door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal with the tall man that you have described? Can you remember if he was wearing uniform or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He was so remarkable and striking that I wouldn't forget him even if I lived for another 50 years. He was tall, a strong man, he was wearing a soldier's cap, a uniform, a life jacket, and he had a moustache, and he was so striking that I don't think it's possible to forget a man like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was his overall attitude that morning, towards the people that he was addressing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I didn't hear him ordering us to be searched, but we were lined up along the wall towards the entrance, or rather the exit, the gate and I'm talking about the side-gate here. And they started searching us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear his name subsequently?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned back from prison and when I bought a TV set in 1993, he was shown on TV and he was arguing on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you hear his name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: A blond, rather nice-looking man, but it was only like that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I'm talking about the tall man with the moustache, did you ever hear the name of that man?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Not until the time when I bought the TV set in 1993. And then he was shown when he was arguing on another bridge, and he was arguing with a peacekeeper. Apparently it was a British peacekeeper, UN TFS staff member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the name that you heard of this tall man?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, it was shown on the news as well, and he was always referred to as Major Sljivancanin. And so it was quite clear that that was the man who was in command at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you saw him on television, this man on television, was that the same man that you believed you saw that morning, the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: 100 per cent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal, if we may, with the exiting from the hospital, and you said that "they" started searching us. Who started searching you? Can you tell the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Since the hospital was surrounded by young soldiers and young soldiers were searching us as well, and some older ones as well. They were looking for weapons, even such things as screwdrivers, knives, bottle openers or whatever, any metal objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you searched?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us then what happened to you after you had been searched, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Nothing special. I had quite a bit of money in my two pockets and the money was given to me by a member of hospital staff because she had too much. And I heard, once we had all been searched, I heard Major Sljivancanin say that we should be put on buses, that was his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And to whom did he give that command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: To somebody who didn't seem to have a rank, he was about 40 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In any event, as a result of that command were you placed on a bus along with others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. As buses were loaded they would drive on a little bit. And some people who worked at the hospital had no IDs, so they too were forced on to these buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How many buses did you see at that time outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Six buses and the licence plates were Zrenjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will deal with the licence plate now, but I will come and deal with the people with no ID. How is it you know what the licence plates were that morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Quite simply, as I was getting on the bus the other bus drove on ahead a little bit, and I looked at the licence plates and I could see, and also I used to work at the CasnaTrans [phoen] warehouse for a while in the past, and so I was interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where is this particular licence plate location? Can you tell us if it's Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Look, since Yugoslavia at that time was still intact, and I was interested in football, and that club, presumably called Proleter from Zrenjanin, was always competing with Borovo in the second division, so that's somewhere near Belgrade near Baca, somewhere near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us that you were placed on the bus and you also told us that some people from the hospital or some people who work the at the hospital had no IDs and so they were forced on to these buses. That is the evidence you have given. Can you remember any of the names of the people who were forced on to the buses, the people who had no IDs from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I'm just going to say a couple of words about why they didn't have any ID. They didn't need it initially, but since there was a lot of shelling day after day, and they no longer had any homes to go to, and let me come back to your original question. I do remember that there was a person called Varenica. I think he was a log smith at the hospital. And there was somebody called Vlaho, he was the driver, he used to drive the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal with the bus that you got on, so I just want to talk about your bus. How many people, approximately, were on your bus when it drove off?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: That bus had about 40 seats, roughly speaking, don't take my word for it, there may have been 48. But there were certainly 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we deal with that bus, are you able to say the ethnicity of the people on that bus as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: 90 per cent Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to assist us, the balance of how many male, how many female, were on your bus as far as you were able to assess?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: In all of those six buses -- well there was only one woman, and her name was Dragica Tuskan. And as to another woman, Markobasic, I'm not sure, but I saw her at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with the buses themselves? Are you able to say what time it was the bus left the JNA -- sorry, left the hospital to go to the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: One by one they retreated by about 20 metres, and it was at about quarter past 9.00, and then they set off in the direction of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Prior to leaving the hospital, and when I say leaving I mean leaving on the buses, did you see any monitors, international monitors at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, I did not see them. There was nobody on that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us move on then, please, to the JNA barracks. Now, just dealing with the bus itself, can you remember if there were any soldiers, JNA soldiers inside the bus?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: There were two young soldiers on every bus, at the doors of the bus. We reached the barracks, we stopped in a circle and I was on the fourth bus and they were parked in the shape of a crescent, and for about 20 minutes nobody was allowed on the buses. There were soldiers, regular soldiers, as well as reservists all around. As well as the paramilitaries. Because I knew quite a few of them. For example, my neighbour, Djuro Latinovic, he was showing his knife and making gestures, indicating that he would slit my throat and cut off my head, and then Bulic Milos Milan, he was shouting, "What is it, Beli? There is no more soccer at the pond." After those 20 minutes a soldier got on the bus. Professor Licina, who was a math teacher, got off and Hadzija and Kolesar who was the husband of the head nurse at the hospital, Biba. Thereupon I saw them dragging other people outside. My first thought was, lucky them, somebody must have rescued them. 10 seconds later I changed my mind as I saw them being beaten up ferociously. They were kicked, beaten by rifle-butts, and punched. And that military bus was not all that big and it drove out of the barracks and turned left in the direction of Negoslavci, as we used to say. At that very moment you all know that barracks have fire extinguishers in case of fire, then they have sandbags and all that, so they smashed all that. They took the handles off spades and rakes and all the other implements and shovels, and they pushed a cry like an Indian tribe who managed to get their hands on a cowboy and it was a kind of a jubilation, and they got into a Yugo car, some five or six of them crowded into that car, and they drove behind the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to just deal with that part of the evidence, which has been of course quite a long answer. You have told us that the buses parked in a semi-circle, and you have told us also about after 20 minutes a soldier getting on to the bus. Were you able or are you able to tell us to what unit the soldier who got on the bus belonged to? Whether he was regular JNA, TOs, or paramilitaries? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I can't really confirm it now, because back then I wasn't too sure what it was, but the person was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the barracks and pulled up in this semi-circle, were there any people outside who saw your buses arrive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I didn't see it because I was sitting behind a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can you tell us then, please, about the people who were being taken off the bus? You've told us about Kolesar, and Latina [sic], and I believe Hamzija, is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I mentioned Latinovic walking around the bus and threatening us with a knife. And Professor Licina, Hidek, and Kolesar, who was the head nurse's, Biba's husband who worked at the hospital and they got off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what happened to them when they got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, where did they then go after they were taken off the bus?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you have told us in your evidence that you saw them being taken off the bus, and then it seems to me that you suggested that you saw them being beaten. Now, I don't know whether it's translation or the way I've put the question. Can you clarify that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I didn't see the three of them being beaten, but the ones who were on the buses, number 1, 2 and 3. They were being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the buses, numbers 1, 2 and 3, where were the people being beaten? Outside or inside the bus?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: On the military buses when they were being loaded or made to board those buses, that is to say the seventh bus, the special military bus, and it has nothing to do with the other six buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But can I just stop you for a moment? You have told us that you pulled up into a semi-circle, you have told us that some people got off your bus, you have told us the names, and you've told us that you had seen other people being beaten towards a military bus. Now, you've not told us about the military bus. Where did the military bus come from? Can you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He was parked there at the barracks. It was -- it was there already, that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you see how many people were being placed on that military bus, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Between 12 and 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the people who were being placed on the military bus, how were they being treated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I think this is what I've already mentioned; very badly, very ferociously. And so I changed my mind straight away, the minute I saw them being punched, hit by rifle-butts, kicked and pushed about, so you can only imagine how bad it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the question I have for you is this: Who was doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: The soldiers who were at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you -- you've already told us that you saw some young JNA soldiers. Are you able to tell us whether there were regular JNA soldiers at the barracks when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that there were two young soldiers on each bus, and there were soldiers in the barracks, of course, as well. And they were talking around and they were watching the scene, and they were there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did any of those soldiers stop the men from being beaten?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, no, no. Not at all. Those people who had been beaten will not live to tell the story, they're not there. I found them at Ovcara. Their heads were all swollen up, they were covered in blood, they were fainting several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I would like you please, just to listen to the question, because I try and keep my questions in compartments. We're talking about the JNA barracks only at this time, and I have asked you, did you see any of the JNA soldiers try to stop the beating, just at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I already said that. I said that nobody tried to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: If we set out at 9.15 from the hospital and arrived at Ovcara at 1330, that means roughly four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about a man called Latinovic. Now, how was Latinovic behaving through this period at the JNA barracks only?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He went around the buses, threatened, but he wasn't alone doing that. There were some 15 men doing that; however he is my neighbour, that's why I remembered him. He lived three houses away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the people who were with Latinovic, were they in uniform or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: They were in uniforms. Bulic Milos was there as well. His name is Milan Bulic Milos, he did not have a uniform. Zoric was there as well, as was Mugosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how were they behaving to the people in the buses? Can you tell the Court exactly how it was they were behaving and what you felt, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: They didn't get on my bus, which was the fourth bus. Only one soldier got on, the one who took those three off the bus. As far as I remember, Bulic, Zoric, or his sons, did not get on the bus. However, there was a lot of screaming because those were the ones who were busy with something else, they were destroying fire extinguishers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us move on, if we can, please, to Ovcara. Now, you've told us that you got to Ovcara at about 1.30 in the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you able to see if the same buses who had pulled up in the semi-circle also went as a group to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I naturally saw that. We were taken by a military vehicle called Campagnola, which is a kind of a combat vehicle, a military vehicle, that's what it's called, Campagnola. They were in front, and we were behind. Young soldiers were still on the buses with us at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, then, with your arrival at Ovcara? You have told us 1.30. Why do you think that you arrived at around about 1.30?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Because I had a pocket-watch, and I looked at it. The sun was high up. It was a lovely day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How long did you stay on the buses at Ovcara? I'm just talking about yourself and your bus at the moment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: About 10 minutes. Until those in front of us were unloaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you were unloaded, what happened to you, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I went out through the back door. Right next to that door was my neighbour, Goran Mugosa, nicknamed Kustro, who was 21 years old. He was in civilian clothes. Around him was a ditch, a type of a ditch full of things, items. Personal IDs, bags, small suitcases, and many other items that people had taken along. I stood next to Mugosa, spread my arms, and then he searched my pockets and took from two pockets a large amount of money which wasn't mine. They belonged to a nurse from the hospital. Then I went to go to the gauntlet, which was eight metres away. And then they got to me with their shoes, fists into my face. I was hit on the head by Dado Djukic next to my right ear, who had crutches because he had been wounded in the leg. My head split open right away. It was only God who saved me from falling down. I have no idea how I managed to get inside. And then Damjan [phoen], Gaspar and another young man, they had been severely beaten at the entrance into the hangar with sticks and other implements. Once I entered and saw Zeljko Begov my neighbour, a young chap,, then I also saw Ante Bodruzic, they had been brought in there earlier in the military vehicle. Their heads were swollen up twice the regular size, their own mothers would not have recognised them. And also other men whose last names I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal now with that evidence that you've given? You have told us that you got off a bus and you have described a gauntlet. What do you mean by a gauntlet? Can you describe to this Court what it is you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, a gauntlet, how shall I describe this to you? On the left and on the right, on both sides of the hangar entrance there were four to five men lined. Let's say there was a total of 10 of them. It was impossible for anyone to enter without them beating you severely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who was in the gauntlet? I don't mean whether you recognised anyone, we'll deal with that later, but were they civilians, were they military, were they wearing uniforms, can you describe to the Court who was actually inside or involved in the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Milos Bulic, Milan, who did not have a uniform, and the Mugosa kid who had taken money from me, and this is something he admitted in Belgrade, only them, the rest were in uniforms. Next to them were young soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see if the young soldiers tried to stop the beatings given out as you went through the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No. Only one soldier took Vile Karlovic aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how hard were these people in the gauntlet hitting the individual who were coming from the bus into the hangar? Can you describe to this Court how severe the beatings were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I don't know if the civilised world will be able to comprehend this. It is very difficult to describe this. You can't even see this in the movies, the beatings were terrible. People lost their teeth. There was so much blood, once we entered the hangar this straw was strewn on the floor and it was all covered in blood, it's hard to describe it. They were kicking, hitting, yelling, screaming, saying, "Ustashas, fuck your mothers," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to help us or to inform us whether all the people who came from the buses went through that gauntlet into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, yes, everybody did. Somebody took longer to enter the hangar and somebody went in quicker, some even fell. When my turn came they had already disembarked three buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about what you have described as the military bus, and you have described seeing someone that you knew whose head was twice the size that it normally would be. Now, do you remember giving that evidence about 10 minutes ago? Can you remember if you saw --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember if you saw any other people from that military bus who were also in the Ovcara hangar when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I was born in Vukovar, and I can tell you that I recognised almost 100 of them, however, I didn't know all of their names. These were young lads, they could have been my sons. I was a friend of their father's. There was some even 16-year-olds there, and there were some people who were 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how would you describe their physical condition when you arrived at the hangar? You've told us about one whose head was twice its normal size, what about the condition of the others? Had they been beaten or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: All I know is that Ante Bodruzic, his head was twice the regular size, his eyes were shut, Zeljko Begov, the same. The other lads who were roughly their age were lads of some 27 years. Zeljko Begov was my neighbour, so it was easy for me to recognise him. As for Ante Bodruzic, he had brought some furniture to my shop to reupholster it, this is how I got to know him. There were some other fellows there, but I wasn't able to register all of them and remember them, however I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us just deal, please, with the inside of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I'm looking at the time, and we've got about three minutes left on the tape. Seeing you're moving to a new subject, I think we'd better break at this point. We will have an adjournment now for 20 minutes or so and resume at 6.00, so that will give you a chance to have a little break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just return, please, to the topic that I had mentioned to you just before the adjournment, and that is I want to deal with inside the hangar at Ovcara. So just deal, if we may, with that one topic. When you went into the hangar itself, were there any people already in there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: There were very many people there inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would you be able to -- would you be able to assess the number of number who were already inside when you went in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I reasoned along these lines: If we had six buses with 40 seats each, that means 240. So there were perhaps 260 to 270 of us, and that is my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I think you were not the last to go in; is that right? I think you -- were you on the third bus?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, I was on the fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if you were on the fourth bus how many people were inside the hangar when you went in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Listen, Your Honour, there were people, and let's say 150. About that's how many. Because there are tears running down your face, blood is rolling down on the right side, your knees are shaking. To tell you the truth, I had no time to count. My rough assessment, 150, 140. You get inside, and -- heads down, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why were your heads down, or was your head down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: First of all, I kept my head down because the young fellow Zeljko Begov fell down, and I helped him up. I and another young lad, I can't remember him now. Let me mention this, I never told his mother what her son had looked like. Everything I saw outside was before I got inside the hangar. Once I got inside the hangar I moved to the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell to this Court, as best you can, what it was like inside that hangar when you went in? What was the atmosphere like? Can you paint a picture for us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: It was a miserable atmosphere. People screaming, beatings, yelling, trampling on people, hitting them with iron rods, with rifle-butts, kicking them, various implements. And then kicking again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that there was straw in the middle and I think you've described blood on it. Can you tell us where all this blood was coming from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. It came from the fellows who had been beaten who was on the military bus. All of them had been severely beaten, based on what I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that you went into the middle of the hangar, and you have also described that you kept your head down. What about other people who came from your bus, did you see what was happening to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I didn't keep my head down the whole time. Naturally at one point I put it up. After me, Mr. Emil Cakalic came in, whom I have known for 40 years. It is easy for me to describe a person I know. Right then, when he ran in, after the first beating outside, which I didn't see, naturally, Slavko Dokmanovic, who used to work with him for municipality, I heard him say, "Oh, Mr. Inspector, you're here as well." And then five of them descended on him and started hitting him. And then after that Dokmanovic kicked -- just a minute, I'm trying to remember the name. Kicked Dado Djukic in the face. Dado had been wounded in his leg, so he was crouching down. And outside of the hangar they beat me with his crutches, they beat me on the head. As far as I remember next to him was -- I'm not a hundred per cent sure about this, young Baumgertner who was a 16-year-old lad. He ran in next to him. I didn't tell his parents either, the fate he suffered there. And then Dokmanovic, trying to imitate a footballer, kicking a ball over the head, hit this boy on the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you about your own injuries at that time? What injuries had you suffered as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: If you add Ovcara and Sremska Mitrovica, then you'll see that I have a defective right ear shell, and then my right eye has a problem. I -- my eyesight is somewhat impaired on the right eye, and it's always bloody because they kicked me wherever they could. In addition to that, I am not allowed to watch any war movies, I shouldn't be in the vicinity of any fighting, physical fighting, and I have trouble sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us that you saw Milan Bulic there. I just want to deal with that person. Did you see him beating any person or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know in my previous statements, which I have been giving for 14 years now, Milan Bulic beat in front of the hangar. I don't know what Damir Samardzic did to him. I told him this in Belgrade, what on earth has he done to you for you to beat him so severely, to beat him to death?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just explain to you, this Court and the Judges will not know what you have said in Belgrade, and therefore it's important that you tell this court exactly what you saw Bulic do. So you are giving your evidence again. Do you understand? So would you be kind enough, please, to tell the Court what it is you saw him do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He met people by the bus, kicked them. There were five of them hitting people. Hitting them with wooden sticks. Whoever they could get their hands on. This lasted until the last person went inside. Sinisa Glavasevic, the journalist, was among the last ones. 12 people descended on him inside the hangar. I don't know what happened to him outside, but they beat him, kicked him, did all sorts of things to him there. At one point in time we could hear a whistle, and this was a man of some 40 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal, please, with two specific topics and then we'll come to the man with the whistle. I know it's difficult to be interrupted, but perhaps it's necessary. Can we deal with Samardzic, the beating of Samardzic, just that and that alone. Can you describe to this Court the ferocity of the beating of that man?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: If I had to show it to you properly I would have to start kicking the tables and the chairs. It was horrible. Following the second punch he fell to the ground, and he was beaten up so badly that after two hours when I went out of the hangar, he couldn't move and his step-son Gaspar also -- I mean, there was a man with his head in a ditch and he was lying down and his legs were resting on the bridge, and they gave no signs of life. I can't describe it any better. You can imagine how it must have been. I mean, five or six of them were beating people one by one, and those people never got up again, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, please, with journalist that you have told us about? Glavasevic, now, how was he attacked, Glavasevic, how was he attacked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: So as to avoid any misunderstandings, Sinisa Glavasevic, who was a Radio Vukovar journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, that was the one. Can you tell us how he was attacked and tell the Court how that occurred and where it occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: When he rushed in already by the door he couldn't even make three steps forward want hangar, I mean. He was beaten by rifle-butts and handles of automatic weapons, and he was beaten on his head, on his legs and he was beaten to the ground. And as far as I can remember, I think they used iron bars and rods and they beat him with that. So you can only imagine how it was. It was horrible, just beyond words. There was no mercy. It is undescribable. What could we have done to him in order for them to want to beat us up so badly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have used the word "they" beat him. Who beat him, what do you mean by the word "they"? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: All those were in uniform. So when I say "they," I mean reservists, paramilitaries, devil will know, I mean there were five different uniforms there, but they were all mixed up together and they were all participating in that beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you at any time see anyone in uniform try to stop these beatings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: If only. If only I were able to tell you that anyone moved their little finger. Nobody, no one at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with a piece of evidence you gave about five minutes ago, and that refers to a gentleman who was blowing a whistle. Do you follow? So I just want to deal with that topic, if I may. So when was the first time that you became aware of someone blowing a whistle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, it was at the time when Slavko Dokmanovic, first of all I could see him and then all of a sudden he disappeared and I couldn't see him anymore. And then somebody else came in, I can claim that he was a reservist, whether he was JNA or not, but he was wearing a reservist uniform and he had a whistle and he came in and he had a whistle like a soccer referee and he was blowing into that whistle, and he said, "That's enough." And at that moment I want to think "oh, thank God," but then another eight people came in and those who were there before went out. And then the next group started the beatings and the same situation started all over again, the screams and so on. And Kemo started shouting "Where is the Francuci?," the Frenchmen. And he was trampling on this young boy, I'm 90 per cent certain that it is Baumgertner, that is his name and he is 16 years old, I know his parents quite well, his father and his mother. But we were all covered in blood, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to deal with the blowing of the whistle and then saying, "That's enough." Who was the man with the whistle speaking to when he said, "That's enough"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: A man wearing a uniform. He could have been 40 years old. I was 50 at the time, going on to 51, and he might have been 41, but in my view he could have been slightly younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. But the question that I asked, and perhaps it was the way I phrased it, is I want to know, you have told us about the man, this man of perhaps 40 years of age, you've told us that he was saying to someone, "That's enough," he's using the phrase, "That's enough." Who is he telling to stop? Who are they? What are they? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He was saying that to the ones who were inside and who were beating us up. The selfsame soldiers who were massacring us. The same uniformed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The uniformed people who were inside that hangar, can you give us an idea of the age range of the people inside the hangar? And I'm only talking about the military, I'm not talking about the people who have come from the bus. Do you understand? So I don't want to know about the people who have come from the bus, I want know about the people who are actually in there in uniform or linked with the uniformed people. Do you follow me? What sort of age span was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, approximately we're talking about an age span between 24 and 44, not counting Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we deal, then, please, with the piece of evidence you gave about where is the Frenchman? Now, did you understand what they meant by the phrase, "Where's the Frenchman?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: As far as I could gather, the one who said, "Where's the Frenchman?" And then the guy came forward and he said here I am. Well, his left hand was bad, and when he was kicked and beaten, he said, "Kemo is going to show you" otherwise I wouldn't know have known the man who said "Where is the Frenchman?" was Kemo, otherwise I wouldn't have known. But after I was released from Mitrovica, Kemo was a trainer at Jakapovac [phoen], and so he was shouting at him, "Kemo is going to show you" and "fuck your mother and father," and then he proceeded to beat him up and you know everybody who came through their hands met with the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But do you know the name of the person who was called the Frenchman? Not the person who attacked, the person who was called the Frenchman? Or do you know the name of the family?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think it's the same boy that was punched in the face, or rather kicked in the face by Slavko Dokmanovic. He must have been 16 or 17 years old, called Banhurta [phoen]. He was a good-looking guy, medium height.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There may be a slight error in the translation. Can you repeat the name of the boy again, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Baumgertner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us about the beatings that you received at the hangar and at Sremska Mitrovica. I want you to forget about the beating at Sremska Mitrovica, I just want to deal only with the beatings you received at the hangar. Do you understand? Only the hangar. Can you tell us, then, please, how you were assaulted in the hangar at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I wasn't kicked or beaten in the hangar because I moved towards the middle of the hangar, but I was beaten up outside. And the ones who were the last to arrive and as the others were doing the beatings were circling around them, well so the last ones to arrive had a pretty bad time of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us that you were beaten outside. Can you tell the Court how it was you ended up moving from the inside of the hangar to the outside of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I can say that I got off the bus through the back door next to Mugosa for that control. And then after five or six metres I reached the people who were waiting for us at the entrance into the hangar and when they fell upon me it was pretty bad in the lower body. They kicked me with their shoes, they had heavy shoes, and one of them wanted to punch me in the head, and then one used Dado Djukic's crutches to hit me on the head and another one kicked me in the back. And they were so quick and I can't even tell you how fast it all went and it was only my good luck, let me emphasise this again, that I didn't fall to the ground and I managed to run into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How long did you actually stay in the hangar? I know it's difficult to assess, but how long do you think?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I can give a pretty good assessment of that. We get there at 1.30, and we came out just before 4.00, 4.00 p.m. I remember quite well, as we were leaving Ovcara, the same kind of polo van was driving in from the opposite direction and the headlights were on already. But it quite dark, but when we reached Velepromet, it was completely dark. So let's say two hours. We spent two hours at Ovcara, we can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can we just deal with it perhaps this way, that when you came out of Ovcara you saw cars with lights on; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Not quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with the natural lighting. How was the natural lighting outside? Was it bright daylight, was it dark, just try and give us an indication, as the Court will hear other evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I can tell you quite easily. My statement was this: Just before 1600 hours, 4.00 p.m., it was still daylight, but as we were leaving Ovcara and we were halfway to Velepromet, and at that stage the car driving from the opposite direction had the lights on. So it wasn't fully dark, but there wasn't a great deal of daylight either. Within six minutes we got there, I mean in front of the Velepromet, and then it was already dark. So darkness fell quite early, at around 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we get to Velepromet, I'd like to deal with how it was that you were taken or came out of the hangar. So there you are in the hangar, and you've told us that you came out of the hangar. How did that occur?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Not a long time after the beatings a soldier came along and asked Miroslav Perkovic, where is Beli, and I said, "Here I am". And it was Dr. Ivankovic's son. He took Stjepan Guncevic, myself and myself out and Zoric took Cakalic out because he was his brother-in-law's friend and Cakalic's brother-in-law was a Serb. As far as I knew, because Zoric was a neighbour of mine, and Zarko Kojic and Miroslav Perkovic and somebody called Dudas came out with us and Vili Karlovic was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was any explanation given to you why it was you were being brought outside?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, I was not given any explanation. I was a pretty good friend with Dr. Ivankovic, his father, and it was not just my case, he was a sociable guy, and he was very approachable for common people, your average man on the street, such as I was. And he didn't have any airs and graces, he didn't keep telling us that he was a high-ranking surgeon and I was just a middle-class decorator, or whatever. And his son might have recognised me, even as I was on the bus, I can't tell you. I mean I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we deal with your trip back to Velepromet? Can you remember approximately how many people travelled back to Velepromet from the hangar itself? And when I refer to those people, I refer to those people travelling with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I think six, but if not I can try and count again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us the names of the people who travelled with you, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I remember very well. Emil Cakalic, Stjepan Guncevic, Drago Berghofer, that is to say myself, Dudas, Miroslav Perkovic, Vili Karlovic, and Zarko Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, before we start dealing with Velepromet, I want to deal with one document that you created yesterday, and I would like you to look at this document, please. It's the number 04680147. I don't know if we're going to be lucky enough to see that on the e-court. If there is not, we have got hard copies. At least I hope we have. I'm going to reach a hard copy to you. It's really not fair for you to be shown something like that. Would the Court object to a photocopy being given to this witness? Now, the Defence have seen this document, and whose handwriting is it? It's a photocopy by the way, but whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: My own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look top right-hand corner we can see the 28th, the 2nd. Which was yesterday, and I think it's right to say that's your signature; is that right? If you look at the paper copy, Mr. Berghofer, I suggest it may help you more than the electronic version, despite what many people think. Now, could you look at the paper that's in your hand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's the same, one is shown on the screen, but you have the luxury of having a photocopy of it as well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask, if I may, please, about this document, we can see that there are numbers 1 to 30. Do you see that on the left-hand side, just keep looking at the paper copy. Now you've got numbers 1 to 30, and we've got various names that you have written down. Who are these people whose names you have written down on this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I say that, I have two more names I testified before the court in order for their mothers to get damages, they're called Jovanovic, and Tomislav Pap. He used to work at the hospital for Dr. Bosanac in the storeroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but can we just deal with the question that I ask you? And that is you've got numbers 1 to 30, you've got the names of people in your handwriting. Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: The first one, Dragan Gavric, Pavo's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I stop you there before we go through every 30, if we deal with the 30 names, would you look at the paper, would you be kind enough? Not the screen. Can we just look at the paper that's in front of you, that's the same thing. Now, all of these names, where did you see all these 30 or 32 people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Let me stress, Your Honours, I've seen quite a few of them, many more that I knew, but I can't remember their family names, I saw them at Ovcara in the same group that I was in, around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, when you compiled this particular list, did you do that from a document or did you do it from memory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: On the basis of my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if the Defence want to ask you any questions about these people, would you be able to assist them in telling them where these people were at Ovcara and what happened to them, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, any time. This list exists and it's dated the 29th of March [as interpreted] 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I want you -- I want you to look at the list you have in front of you, the paper document. The date on that --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The date on that is the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: The 28th of February of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And how did you compile this list? How did you come to write it all down? Can you tell the Court? You say that you saw them at Ovcara. Why did you write this list out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. Just to show you that all of these people were people that I know who were my neighbours, and they're the same victims named at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just clear up one matter that may cause a question, it's simply this: You have told us about a list in 1992, and you remember saying that about two minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What list is that that was created in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: The first day when I came to Hotel Plitvice in Zagreb after being in jail in Mitrovica, I was given a piece of paper and I immediately set out to write this, and I didn't even make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say, is it not, that that particular list is not with you, that I think it is back in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No. That's correct, I wrote it based on what I remembered, based on my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I please put this list, which was created yesterday and signed and dated by this witness as an exhibit demonstrating the names of people that he saw at Ovcara when he was there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a list based on his memory here in The Hague in the last few days or is it based on some earlier document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's not for me to give evidence, but can I just say that it is a document that is created from his memory yesterday without any reference to the other list. So it is basically a memory document created yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number 228.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal then, please, with Velepromet. You say that you were taken to Velepromet that evening. Did you actually go into the Velepromet facility that night or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: We didn't, we stopped in front of the gate. There was no room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where did you go after Velepromet, if there was no room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we went towards Petrovci. To a clothing factory called Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you stay the night at Modateks or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, as far as you are aware, was that the same group that had left with you from Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you leave Modateks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: When we spent the night between the 20th and the 21st in the morning Zeljko Mudri arrived, my colleague and a school friend. And took to Dudas. Somebody came to fetch Zarko Kojic, it may have been his grandmother. But Zarko Kojic left us on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you ever return to the Velepromet facility that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: We did. On that day, which was the 21st of November, at around 1530 or 1600 hours, between 3.00 and 4.00 p.m., it was still daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm going to move on to the topic of Velepromet, JNA barracks and one or two other general topics. I appreciate it's six minutes early, I can take the witness on that topic if you wish, but it might be a suitable place to adjourn this evening so that he can deal with the matter cleanly in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn at this stage. We continue tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. Could I mention it will be necessary for the Chamber to finish the sitting at 1.15 tomorrow, as there is a visiting group of judges that we must meet at that time. So we will sit from 9.00 until 1.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.52 p.m.,
